screens.title: Advanced Data Structures and Gas Optimization
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will explore how your choice and layout of data in Solidity directly change the gas cost users pay. Gas is a real monetary cost on Ethereum, so efficient contracts are more usable and sustainable. You will learn when mappings beat arrays, how struct member order enables storage packing, and why choosing storage, memory, or calldata matters for each function call. I will show concrete examples, including a small UserProfile contract that demonstrates packing benefits and safe update patterns. We'll also review common gas-heavy operations like writing storage, unbounded loops, and frequent external calls, and then practice strategies such as minimizing storage writes, caching values in memory, using calldata for read-only inputs, and using events instead of storing historical logs. By the end of this chapter you should be able to choose data layouts and function patterns that lower SSTORE counts and avoid costly runtime loops. Consider a simple mapping of balances: by using a mapping you get constant-time lookup without iteration, which is often the most gas-efficient choice when you don’t need enumeration. Keep this question in mind as we go: which data location and packing choice saves the most gas for a given operation?

Advanced Data Structures and Gas Optimization

Design decisions about mappings, structs, arrays, and data locations change how many storage slots your contract uses and how often SSTORE runs. This slide deck makes those effects tangible and actionable.

In this lesson
Measure and reduce SSTOREs through packing and calldata choices.
Coming up
Examples: UserProfile packing and optimizing loops.
Why it matters
Lower gas increases adoption and reduces user friction.
Visual summary
Cards show where costs come from
Mappings: fast lookup
Constant access cost, not iterable.
Structs: pack fields
Order members to pack into single slot.
Arrays: watch iteration
Unbounded loops can exhaust gas.
Tip: plan data layout early. Small changes to ordering save repeated SSTORE costs for all users.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives break the chapter into practical skills you can apply when writing Solidity. First, you will choose the most appropriate data structure — mapping, struct, or array — based on access patterns and gas implications, for example using a mapping for frequent address lookups where enumeration is unnecessary. Second, you will understand storage packing and how ordering small fields together reduces storage slots; a concrete example is grouping uint8 values so the compiler fits them into a single 32-byte slot. Third, you will identify gas-expensive operations like SSTORE, external calls, and unbounded loops, and recognize when those operations threaten transaction success. Fourth, you will learn to pick between storage, memory, and calldata for function inputs and temporary variables, such as declaring external read-only arrays as calldata to reduce copy costs. Each objective focuses on a practical change you can make in your contract to lower costs while maintaining security and clarity.

screens.title: Mappings — Efficient key-value storage
screens.narratorSegment: Mappings are a specialized key-value store in Solidity with two important gas characteristics. First, accessing or writing a mapping entry has a fixed gas cost that does not grow with the number of elements. That makes mappings ideal for frequent lookups keyed by a unique identifier — for example, balances keyed by an address. Second, mappings are not iterable and have no built-in length, which is a trade-off: you avoid iteration cost but you cannot enumerate keys on-chain. A common misconception is to use a dynamic array to store keys and a mapping for values together; while this allows iteration, it introduces additional storage writes for the array and increases gas. If you do need enumeration, consider off-chain indexing, events, or explicit pagination rather than maintaining a growing on-chain list. In practice, mapping(address => uint256) public balances; is an excellent choice when you need constant-time lookups and can accept non-iterability. Example: storing token balances or user profiles by address. Closing question: when would you accept the cost of additional storage to support iteration instead of relying on a mapping? Mappings — Efficient key-value storage means use mappings for constant-time lookups when enumeration is unnecessary; avoid adding an on-chain index unless required.. In practical terms, why mappings are gas-friendly when you avoid iteration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Mappings
Core Concept

Mappings for key-value access

Mappings provide constant-time access by key and avoid iteration, saving gas when enumeration isn't required.

Guide
Access cost is independent of size; no length or iteration.
Misconception
Using an array for iteration adds storage writes and can be far more expensive than alternatives like events or off-chain indexing.
Key Takeaway

Prefer mappings when you need fast lookup and don’t require on-chain enumeration; index only when necessary.

Example
// mapping for balances
mapping(address => uint256) public balances;

function setBalance(address user, uint256 amount) public {
  balances[user] = amount; // single storage write for that key
}

function getBalance(address user) public view returns (uint256) {
  return balances[user]; // constant-time read
}
When to use
User balances, permissions, and any keyed storage where you don't need to iterate all keys.
When to avoid
When you must enumerate all entries on-chain frequently; consider events or off-chain indexing instead.

screens.title: Structs and Storage Packing
screens.narratorSegment: Structs let you group related state variables into a single type, which helps organization and can improve gas when fields are ordered for packing. Solidity packs variables into 32-byte slots when possible. That means smaller types like uint8, uint16, address, and bool can share a single slot if arranged properly. A common rule is to group smaller fields together and place larger 32-byte types, like uint256, after them. For example, uint8 a; uint8 b; uint256 c; will pack a and b into one slot and use a second slot for c. A misconception is thinking that simply using smaller types always reduces gas; the savings come from packing multiple small fields into one slot so fewer SSTOREs occur when writing the struct. Also, writing a whole struct at once can be cheaper than writing separate state variables individually because one assignment uses a single storage write for the packed slot. When designing structs, consider the total byte size and whether fields sum to less than 32 bytes so the compiler can pack them together. This attention to detail reduces storage slots, SSTORE frequency, and therefore gas.

keyIdea.title: Packing principle
keyIdea.text: Group small fields together and place large fields last so the compiler can pack multiple small fields into one 32-byte storage slot, saving gas on writes.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Structs & Packing
Definition

Storage packing explained

Solidity packs smaller fields into a 32-byte slot when possible. Order fields to maximize packing and reduce the number of storage slots.

Packing example
uint8 a; uint8 b; uint256 c; packs a and b together and stores c separately.
Misconception
Smaller types alone don't save gas unless they are arranged to share storage slots.
Key Takeaway

Optimizing struct member order is a simple, repeatable change that reduces storage slots and SSTORE cost across all writes.

Concrete comparison
Inefficient
struct MyData {
  uint256 largeNum;
  bool flag;
  uint8 smallNum;
}
// Uses 3 slots
Efficient
struct MyData {
  bool flag;
  uint8 smallNum;
  uint256 largeNum;
}
// Packs flag+smallNum into one slot; largeNum in another

screens.title: Storage Packing — Example in Solidity
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a concrete code fragment that demonstrates good and bad packing. The example shows a struct and two field orders. When smaller fields are separated by a uint256, the compiler cannot pack them together, increasing storage slots. In contrast, grouping small fields up front allows the compiler to place them in the same 32-byte slot. This is not just theoretical: every additional slot written with SSTORE increases the gas of that transaction. A common pitfall is changing struct layout during upgrades; changing ordering can alter storage layout and break contract state — so plan packing upfront or use upgradeable patterns with care. In practice, writing a packed struct in one assignment reduces the number of SSTORE operations versus writing each field individually. As an exercise, think about a struct that totals 24 bytes: storing it uses one slot, but if you split it across writes, you may cause multiple SSTOREs. The closing question: how would you refactor an existing contract that has separately written fields to minimize SSTOREs without breaking storage layout? Storage Packing — Example in Solidity means reorder struct members and write packed structs in a single assignment to avoid extra sstores; beware of storage layout changes in upgrades.. In practical terms, see how ordering fields affects storage usage. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Packing Walkthrough
Bad packing example
// Bad packing: separated small fields
struct BadUser {
  uint8 age;        // 1 byte
  uint256 balance;  // 32 bytes - takes a full slot
  uint8 score;      // 1 byte - ends up in a new slot
}

// Writing fields separately can trigger multiple SSTOREs
// and cost more gas cumulatively.
Misconception: Using small types guarantees gas savings. The saving only occurs when they occupy the same storage slot.
Good packing example
// Good packing: grouped small fields
struct UserInfo {
  uint8 age;         // 1 byte
  uint8 isActive;    // 1 byte
  uint16 score;      // 2 bytes
  address userAddr;  // 20 bytes
  // Total 24 bytes -> fits in one 32-byte slot
}

// Assigning the whole struct in one write packs into a single slot,
// reducing the number of SSTORE operations.
Tip: group small fields, write packed structs in a single assignment to reduce SSTORE occurrences.

screens.title: Arrays: Fixed-size vs Dynamic
screens.narratorSegment: Arrays appear in two main flavors: fixed-size and dynamic. Fixed-size arrays with a known small bound are often cheaper because the compiler and EVM can make assumptions about storage layout. Dynamic arrays are flexible but come with operational costs: push and pop that allocate or deallocate storage slots, and iteration that grows with array length. Iterating over large dynamic arrays inside a transaction is a frequent source of high gas and even failed transactions. A common misconception is that dynamic arrays are fine if you rarely push; however, when functions iterate over dynamic arrays you expose yourself to gas unpredictability. Alternatives include pagination, where callers process a slice of the array per transaction, or off-chain aggregation where a user queries elements individually or uses events. If you must store a list of keys, consider emitting events and using off-chain indexers rather than maintaining an on-chain array that grows indefinitely. Example pattern: use a dynamic array for small temporary buffers, but for large or unbounded data prefer events and per-index getters. Arrays: Fixed-size vs Dynamic means use fixed-size arrays for small known collections; avoid unbounded iteration on dynamic arrays by paginating or moving aggregation off-chain.. In practical terms, when arrays become expensive and how to avoid pitfalls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Arrays
Fixed-size arrays

Use uint256[5] style arrays for small, predictable collections — predictable storage layout and often cheaper operations.

When to use
Small sets of values known at design time.
Warning
Not flexible for growth; changing size requires migration or redeploy.
Dynamic arrays

Flexible size, but push, pop, and iteration can allocate or traverse many storage slots, raising gas costs.

Common pitfall
Unbounded loops over dynamic arrays can exceed block gas limits and fail transactions.
Alternatives
Use pagination, per-index getters, or events + off-chain indexing for large or growing datasets.
Example scenario

If you need to keep every historical transfer for queries, prefer emitting events and using off-chain tools rather than storing all transfers in a dynamic array on-chain.

screens.title: Data Locations: Storage, Memory, Calldata
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding storage, memory, and calldata is essential to control gas usage in functions. Storage is the persistent on-chain location; any state variable lives here and reading or writing to storage is the most expensive operation. Memory is a temporary area that exists only during a function call and is cheaper than storage; use memory for local variables and for temporary copies of complex types that will not persist. Calldata is a read-only area for external function arguments and is cheaper than memory because it avoids copying for read-only use. A practical rule: declare external function complex inputs such as arrays or structs as calldata if you do not modify them — this reduces copies into memory. A common misconception is that calldata can be written to; it cannot. If you must modify an input, copy it into memory first. Also, repeatedly reading a storage variable in a function is costlier than reading it once into memory and reusing the memory variable; cache expensive reads to save gas. Consider this example pattern: read state into a local variable, perform calculations in memory, then write back a single storage value. Closing question: when would you prefer memory over calldata for an external input?

keyIdea.title: Location rules
keyIdea.text: Use calldata for read-only external inputs, memory for temporary modified copies, and minimize storage reads/writes by caching in memory.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Storage vs Memory vs Calldata
Storage

Persistent & expensive

State variables live here; SSTORE is costly. Minimize writes and group them.

Memory

Temporary & cheaper

Use for local modifications and to cache reads to reduce repeated storage access.

Calldata

Read-only & cheapest

Pass external arrays or structs as calldata when you don't need to modify them.

Example pattern
Cache reads
Load state into a local memory variable and reuse it to avoid multiple SLOADs.
Use calldata
External view functions that accept arrays should use calldata to lower gas for callers.

screens.title: Gas-expensive operations to watch
screens.narratorSegment: Certain operations are consistently expensive and should be minimized or structured carefully. Writing to storage with SSTORE is the most costly operation, particularly when changing a slot from zero to non-zero. Creating new storage slots is expensive, and while deleting a slot yields a partial refund, relying on refunds can be risky. External calls have unpredictable gas costs and can re-enter or fail; minimize or isolate them and avoid calling external contracts inside loops. Loops themselves are dangerous when bounds depend on user-supplied or growing data structures; unbounded loops can exceed the gas limit and make functions unusable. String manipulation is also expensive due to dynamic memory operations. To mitigate these issues, order require checks from cheapest to most expensive so a failing condition aborts early, cache storage reads to memory to avoid multiple SLOADs, and emit events instead of storing large history data. A concrete scenario: if a function must process a dynamic list of user IDs, prefer paginated calls or off-chain aggregation rather than looping across the entire list in one transaction. Reflect: which of these expensive operations appears most in your contracts today and how would you refactor it?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › Gas Hotspots

Gas-expensive operations

Recognize and minimize these to keep transaction costs reasonable.

SSTORE (writing storage)
Most expensive. Minimize writes; prefer single assignments for packed structs.
External calls
Unpredictable gas and reentrancy risks. Avoid inside loops.
Unbounded loops
Can hit gas limits. Use pagination or off-chain processing.
String and dynamic data ops
Dynamic memory and copying are costly; avoid heavy string manipulation on-chain.
Mitigation
Cache reads, write once, and emit events instead of storing large histories.
Pattern
Order require checks cheaply to fail fast and save gas on bad calls.
Check
Avoid external calls in loops; isolate or move them off the critical path.

screens.title: Gas Optimization Strategies
screens.narratorSegment: This screen gathers practical optimization strategies you can apply immediately. First, minimize storage writes: update state only when necessary and prefer writing a packed struct once rather than multiple independent writes. Second, pack storage variables by ordering small members together so they share slots. Third, use calldata for external read-only inputs to avoid copying into memory; when you must modify inputs, copy to memory explicitly. Module 4 › Chapter 3.5 › OptimizedUserProfile
Contract walkthrough
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract OptimizedUserProfile {
    struct UserProfile {
        address userAddress; // 20 bytes
        uint64 userId;       // 8 bytes
        uint16 reputation;   // 2 bytes
        bool isActive;       // 1 byte
        // Total 31 bytes fit in one 32-byte slot
    }

    mapping(address => UserProfile) public profiles;

    function addProfile(address _userAddress, uint64 _userId, uint16 _reputation, bool _isActive) public {
        require(profiles[_userAddress].userAddress == address(0), "Profile already exists.");
        profiles[_userAddress] = UserProfile({
            userAddress: _userAddress,
            userId: _userId,
            reputation: _reputation,
            isActive: _isActive
        });
    }

    function updateReputation(address _userAddress, uint16 _newReputation) public {
        UserProfile storage userProfile = profiles[_userAddress];
        require(userProfile.userAddress != address(0), "Profile does not exist.");
        userProfile.reputation = _newReputation; // single write to packed slot
    }
}
Why this is efficient
Packed struct fits into one slot and mapping lookups are constant-time.
Hands-on task

Moving fields around in a live contract can break storage layout; plan upgrades carefully.

screens.title: Patterns to Avoid: Unbounded Loops & External Calls
screens.narratorSegment: This lesson focuses on patterns that commonly cause failures in production: unbounded loops and external calls inside loops. Unbounded loops over large dynamic arrays can exceed gas limits and cause DoS-like failures for callers. If you find such loops, refactor by implementing pagination — allow callers to process fixed-size slices in multiple transactions — or move aggregation off-chain. When you need to inform many accounts, consider emitting events rather than looping to store data for each account on-chain. External calls are another source of unpredictability; avoid making external contract calls in the critical path of state updates, and never perform untrusted external calls before you update your own state. A useful strategy is the checks-effects-interactions pattern: perform checks, update state, then interact externally. Also, consider batching operations in a way that keeps per-transaction gas bounded. A common mistake is to try to optimize a single call with heavy looping; instead, design APIs that require bounded, predictable work per transaction. Reflect: where could pagination replace a risky loop in your current codebase? fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will explore how your choice and layout of data in Solidity directly change the gas cost users pay. Gas is a real monetary cost on Ethereum, so efficient contracts are more usable and sustainable. You will learn when mappings beat arrays, how struct member order enables storage packing, and why choosing storage, memory, or calldata matters for each function call. I will show concrete examples, including a small UserProfile contract that demonstrates packing benefits and safe update patterns. We'll also review common gas-heavy operations like writing storage, unbounded loops, and frequent external calls, and then practice strategies such as minimizing storage writes, caching values in memory, using calldata for read-only inputs, and using events instead of storing historical logs. By the end of this chapter you should be able to choose data layouts and function patterns that lower SSTORE counts and avoid costly runtime loops. Consider a simple mapping of balances: by using a mapping you get constant-time lookup without iteration, which is often the most gas-efficient choice when you don’t need enumeration. Keep this question in mind as we go: which data location and packing choice saves the most gas for a given operation?

These objectives break the chapter into practical skills you can apply when writing Solidity. First, you will choose the most appropriate data structure — mapping, struct, or array — based on access patterns and gas implications, for example using a mapping for frequent address lookups where enumeration is unnecessary. Second, you will understand storage packing and how ordering small fields together reduces storage slots; a concrete example is grouping uint8 values so the compiler fits them into a single 32-byte slot. Third, you will identify gas-expensive operations like SSTORE, external calls, and unbounded loops, and recognize when those operations threaten transaction success. Fourth, you will learn to pick between storage, memory, and calldata for function inputs and temporary variables, such as declaring external read-only arrays as calldata to reduce copy costs. Each objective focuses on a practical change you can make in your contract to lower costs while maintaining security and clarity.

Continuing the objectives, you will implement gas-efficient loop structures and external call patterns: that means avoiding unbounded loops in frequently called functions, using pagination or off-chain aggregation when possible, and caching storage reads into memory for repeated use within a function. You will also practice strategies such as short-circuiting checks to fail early and save gas, deleting unused storage to claim refunds, and preferring events for historical logs when persistent on-chain read access is unnecessary. Finally, you will be able to apply these tactics in a hands-on activity where you reorder struct fields, use calldata for inputs, and perform single-slot struct writes to reduce SSTORE overhead. These objectives are practical; each one corresponds to a code-level change that lowers transaction cost while preserving correctness and security. Learning Objectives — Practice & Patterns means you will be able to implement safer contract patterns: fail early, cache storage reads, paginate large data, and prefer events when possible.. In practical terms, practical tactics you will apply in code. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Mappings are a specialized key-value store in Solidity with two important gas characteristics. First, accessing or writing a mapping entry has a fixed gas cost that does not grow with the number of elements. That makes mappings ideal for frequent lookups keyed by a unique identifier — for example, balances keyed by an address. Second, mappings are not iterable and have no built-in length, which is a trade-off: you avoid iteration cost but you cannot enumerate keys on-chain. A common misconception is to use a dynamic array to store keys and a mapping for values together; while this allows iteration, it introduces additional storage writes for the array and increases gas. If you do need enumeration, consider off-chain indexing, events, or explicit pagination rather than maintaining a growing on-chain list. In practice, mapping(address => uint256) public balances; is an excellent choice when you need constant-time lookups and can accept non-iterability. Example: storing token balances or user profiles by address. Closing question: when would you accept the cost of additional storage to support iteration instead of relying on a mapping? Mappings — Efficient key-value storage means use mappings for constant-time lookups when enumeration is unnecessary; avoid adding an on-chain index unless required.. In practical terms, why mappings are gas-friendly when you avoid iteration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Structs let you group related state variables into a single type, which helps organization and can improve gas when fields are ordered for packing. Solidity packs variables into 32-byte slots when possible. That means smaller types like uint8, uint16, address, and bool can share a single slot if arranged properly. A common rule is to group smaller fields together and place larger 32-byte types, like uint256, after them. For example, uint8 a; uint8 b; uint256 c; will pack a and b into one slot and use a second slot for c. A misconception is thinking that simply using smaller types always reduces gas; the savings come from packing multiple small fields into one slot so fewer SSTOREs occur when writing the struct. Also, writing a whole struct at once can be cheaper than writing separate state variables individually because one assignment uses a single storage write for the packed slot. When designing structs, consider the total byte size and whether fields sum to less than 32 bytes so the compiler can pack them together. This attention to detail reduces storage slots, SSTORE frequency, and therefore gas.

Let's walk through a concrete code fragment that demonstrates good and bad packing. The example shows a struct and two field orders. When smaller fields are separated by a uint256, the compiler cannot pack them together, increasing storage slots. In contrast, grouping small fields up front allows the compiler to place them in the same 32-byte slot. This is not just theoretical: every additional slot written with SSTORE increases the gas of that transaction. A common pitfall is changing struct layout during upgrades; changing ordering can alter storage layout and break contract state — so plan packing upfront or use upgradeable patterns with care. In practice, writing a packed struct in one assignment reduces the number of SSTORE operations versus writing each field individually. As an exercise, think about a struct that totals 24 bytes: storing it uses one slot, but if you split it across writes, you may cause multiple SSTOREs. The closing question: how would you refactor an existing contract that has separately written fields to minimize SSTOREs without breaking storage layout? Storage Packing — Example in Solidity means reorder struct members and write packed structs in a single assignment to avoid extra sstores; beware of storage layout changes in upgrades.. In practical terms, see how ordering fields affects storage usage. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Arrays appear in two main flavors: fixed-size and dynamic. Fixed-size arrays with a known small bound are often cheaper because the compiler and EVM can make assumptions about storage layout. Dynamic arrays are flexible but come with operational costs: push and pop that allocate or deallocate storage slots, and iteration that grows with array length. Iterating over large dynamic arrays inside a transaction is a frequent source of high gas and even failed transactions. A common misconception is that dynamic arrays are fine if you rarely push; however, when functions iterate over dynamic arrays you expose yourself to gas unpredictability. Alternatives include pagination, where callers process a slice of the array per transaction, or off-chain aggregation where a user queries elements individually or uses events. If you must store a list of keys, consider emitting events and using off-chain indexers rather than maintaining an on-chain array that grows indefinitely. Example pattern: use a dynamic array for small temporary buffers, but for large or unbounded data prefer events and per-index getters. Arrays: Fixed-size vs Dynamic means use fixed-size arrays for small known collections; avoid unbounded iteration on dynamic arrays by paginating or moving aggregation off-chain.. In practical terms, when arrays become expensive and how to avoid pitfalls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Understanding storage, memory, and calldata is essential to control gas usage in functions. Storage is the persistent on-chain location; any state variable lives here and reading or writing to storage is the most expensive operation. Memory is a temporary area that exists only during a function call and is cheaper than storage; use memory for local variables and for temporary copies of complex types that will not persist. Calldata is a read-only area for external function arguments and is cheaper than memory because it avoids copying for read-only use. A practical rule: declare external function complex inputs such as arrays or structs as calldata if you do not modify them — this reduces copies into memory. A common misconception is that calldata can be written to; it cannot. If you must modify an input, copy it into memory first. Also, repeatedly reading a storage variable in a function is costlier than reading it once into memory and reusing the memory variable; cache expensive reads to save gas. Consider this example pattern: read state into a local variable, perform calculations in memory, then write back a single storage value. Closing question: when would you prefer memory over calldata for an external input?

Certain operations are consistently expensive and should be minimized or structured carefully. Writing to storage with SSTORE is the most costly operation, particularly when changing a slot from zero to non-zero. Creating new storage slots is expensive, and while deleting a slot yields a partial refund, relying on refunds can be risky. External calls have unpredictable gas costs and can re-enter or fail; minimize or isolate them and avoid calling external contracts inside loops. Loops themselves are dangerous when bounds depend on user-supplied or growing data structures; unbounded loops can exceed the gas limit and make functions unusable. String manipulation is also expensive due to dynamic memory operations. To mitigate these issues, order require checks from cheapest to most expensive so a failing condition aborts early, cache storage reads to memory to avoid multiple SLOADs, and emit events instead of storing large history data. A concrete scenario: if a function must process a dynamic list of user IDs, prefer paginated calls or off-chain aggregation rather than looping across the entire list in one transaction. Reflect: which of these expensive operations appears most in your contracts today and how would you refactor it?

First, minimize storage writes: update state only when necessary and prefer writing a packed struct once rather than multiple independent writes. Second, pack storage variables by ordering small members together so they share slots. Third, use calldata for external read-only inputs to avoid copying into memory; when you must modify inputs, copy to memory explicitly. Fourth, cache storage reads into memory variables for repeated access inside a function to avoid multiple SLOADs. Fifth, delete unused storage slots when appropriate to receive gas refunds. Sixth, prefer events for historical data that does not need to be read by contracts. Seventh, short-circuit expensive require checks by ordering cheap validations first. Eighth, avoid unbounded loops and implement pagination or off-chain aggregation. A common misconception is that optimizing one small function is enough; optimization must be systematic and measured with a gas profiler. Use tools to measure changes and prioritize fixes that reduce frequent costs for users. Now we will review the provided OptimizedUserProfile contract that puts the chapter's ideas into practice. The struct orders the address first, then smaller numeric types so the total fits within a single 32-byte slot. The mapping stores the packed struct, and addProfile writes the full struct in one assignment, reducing SSTORE counts. This lesson focuses on patterns that commonly cause failures in production: unbounded loops and external calls inside loops. Unbounded loops over large dynamic arrays can exceed gas limits and cause DoS-like failures for callers. If you find such loops, refactor by implementing pagination — allow callers to process fixed-size slices in multiple transactions — or move aggregation off-chain. When you need to inform many accounts, consider emitting events rather than looping to store data for each account on-chain. External calls are another source of unpredictability; avoid making external contract calls in the critical path of state updates, and never perform untrusted external calls before you update your own state. A useful strategy is the checks-effects-interactions pattern: perform checks, update state, then interact externally. Also, consider batching operations in a way that keeps per-transaction gas bounded. A common mistake is to try to optimize a single call with heavy looping; instead, design APIs that require bounded, predictable work per transaction. Reflect: where could pagination replace a risky loop in your current codebase? Let's summarize the essential concepts to remember. First, gas optimization is about reducing expensive operations, primarily storage writes and unbounded computation. Second, mappings provide constant-time lookups with no iteration — ideal for address-keyed data when you don't need enumeration. Third, struct storage packing is a powerful way to reduce slots by ordering small fields together so they fit within a single 32-byte slot. Each of these ideas is practical and measurable: you can use a gas profiler to see SSTORE counts and the effect of packing. Keep in mind trade-offs: packing and using calldata reduce gas, but changing storage layout carelessly can break deployed contracts. Finally, adopt patterns like caching storage reads in memory, using events for logs, pagination for large arrays, and short-circuiting require checks to save gas on failed transactions. These behaviors will make your contracts cheaper and more resilient for users.

Here are three concise reminders to guide your day-to-day Solidity decisions. First, storage writes cost the most: minimize SSTOREs by packing fields and writing packed structs in a single assignment. Second, use data locations wisely: calldata for read-only external inputs, memory for temporary data, and storage only for persistent state. Third, avoid unbounded on-chain work: paginate, emit events for logs, and move heavy aggregation off-chain.
